title: What are the ways to implement a thread-safe Singleton in Java? Compare eager initialization, synchronized getInstance, double-checked locking with volatile, the Bill Pugh holder idiom, and the enum singleton, and say which is preferred.

s1_definition.profdef: A Singleton ensures exactly one instance of a class exists for the whole JVM and provides a global access point to it. Making it thread-safe means guaranteeing that even under concurrent access, only one instance is ever created and all threads see a fully constructed instance. The main approaches are eager initialization (create at class load), a synchronized getInstance method (correct but slow), double-checked locking with a volatile field (fast lazy creation), the Bill Pugh static holder idiom (lazy, fast, no synchronization), and the enum singleton (simplest and safest, also serialization and reflection proof).
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has exactly one central vault for the whole bank. No matter how many tellers ask for it at the same time, there must be only one vault, and it must be fully built before anyone uses it. A Singleton is that one shared vault. Thread safety means that even if ten tellers rush in at the same instant on opening day, they do not accidentally build two vaults or hand someone a half-built vault.
s1_definition.oneliner: For a thread-safe Singleton, prefer the Bill Pugh holder idiom for lazy loading or the enum for the simplest bulletproof version.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Singleton ensures exactly one instance of a class exists for the whole JVM and provides a global access point to it. Making it thread-safe means guaranteeing that even under concurrent access, only one instance is ever created and all threads see a fully constructed instance. The main approaches are eager initialization (create at class load), a synchronized getInstance method (correct but slow), double-checked locking with a volatile field (fast lazy creation), the Bill Pugh static holder idiom (lazy, fast, no synchronization), and the enum singleton (simplest and safest, also serialization and reflection proof).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has exactly one central vault for the whole bank. No matter how many tellers ask for it at the same time, there must be only one vault, and it must be fully built before anyone uses it. A Singleton is that one shared vault. Thread safety means that even if ten tellers rush in at the same instant on opening day, they do not accidentally build two vaults or hand someone a half-built vault.

**One line to remember:** For a thread-safe Singleton, prefer the Bill Pugh holder idiom for lazy loading or the enum for the simplest bulletproof version.

sections.s2_technical:
Eager initialization creates the instance when the class is loaded, with `private static final ConnectionPool INSTANCE = new ConnectionPool();`. The JVM guarantees class initialization is thread-safe, so this is correct with zero synchronization. The only downside is the instance is built even if never used, which wastes resources for an expensive object.

The synchronized getInstance method is lazy and correct but slow. You write `public static synchronized ConnectionPool getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new ConnectionPool(); return instance; }`. Every single call pays the cost of acquiring the lock even long after the instance exists, which is a bottleneck under heavy concurrency.

Double-checked locking with volatile fixes the performance problem. You declare `private static volatile ConnectionPool instance;` and check null without a lock, then lock and check again only if it is null. The `volatile` keyword is mandatory here, because without it another thread could see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor has not finished, due to instruction reordering. With volatile, the safe-publication guarantee holds. The first null check avoids locking once the instance exists.

The Bill Pugh holder idiom uses a private static inner class that holds the instance. The inner class is not loaded until `getInstance` first references it, so initialization is lazy, and the JVM's class-initialization lock makes it thread-safe without any explicit synchronization in your code. For example `private static class Holder { static final ConnectionPool INSTANCE = new ConnectionPool(); }` and `return Holder.INSTANCE;`. This is the idiom most senior engineers prefer when they want laziness.

The enum singleton, recommended by Joshua Bloch, is the simplest and most robust: `public enum ConnectionPool { INSTANCE; ... }`. The JVM guarantees a single instance, and uniquely it is also safe against serialization attacks and reflection attacks that can create a second instance of the other forms. Its only limitation is that an enum cannot extend a class. A senior nuance is that the other forms need a `readResolve` method and defenses to stay single under serialization and reflection, whereas the enum gets all of that for free.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India uses a single shared database connection pool for its transfer service. Creating the pool is expensive, so it must be created once and reused. In an early version two threads called getInstance at the same instant and each created its own pool, so the bank briefly ran two pools and exhausted the database connection limit. This is exactly the thread-safe Singleton problem — concurrent creation must yield exactly one instance.

Problem 2 — The team also needed the pool to survive serialization in a cache without accidentally creating a second copy. This is exactly what the enum singleton solves for free.

The project demonstrates a connection pool as a Singleton in all five forms. `EagerPool` is eager. `SyncPool` uses synchronized getInstance. `DclPool` uses double-checked locking with volatile. `HolderPool` uses the Bill Pugh idiom. `EnumPool` is the enum. The demo hammers each with many threads and confirms only one instance is created.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: 50 threads simultaneously call `DclPool.getInstance()` after a shared latch is released.

Step 1 — All 50 threads block on `start.await()`. The main thread calls `start.countDown()`, releasing them at the same instant to maximize contention.

Step 2 — Each thread runs the first null check `if (instance == null)`. On the very first race, many threads see null because nobody has created the instance yet.

Step 3 — The threads that saw null compete for the lock on `DclPool.class`. Exactly one wins, enters the synchronized block, re-checks null, sees null, and creates the single instance. Because the field is volatile, the fully constructed instance is safely published.

Step 4 — The remaining threads that were waiting on the lock enter one by one, re-check null, now see a non-null instance, and skip creation. Threads that had not yet reached the lock see non-null on the first check and never lock at all.

Step 5 — Every thread records the instance id into a concurrent set. Because there is exactly one instance, the set contains exactly one id.

Final output:

```
DclPool unique ids under load: 1
HolderPool id: 85203114771200
EnumPool id:   85203114782100
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  50 threads call DclPool.getInstance() at once
    │
    ▼
  first check: instance == null ?
    │
    ├─ null (racing threads)                 ├─ non-null (later threads)
    │    │                                   │   return existing instance
    │    ▼                                   │   (NO lock — hot path)
    │  synchronized(DclPool.class)           │
    │    │  second check: still null ?       │
    │    ├─ yes → new DclPool()  ───┐        │
    │    │        volatile write    │        │
    │    └─ no  → skip              │        │
    ▼                               ▼        ▼
  ────────── exactly ONE instance published ──────────
  unique id set size = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Singleton guarantees exactly one instance of a class for the entire JVM and gives a global access point to it. Making it thread-safe means that even when many threads call for it at the same instant, only one instance is ever created and every thread sees a fully constructed object. I know five ways to do this and I choose based on whether I need lazy loading and how much robustness I want.

Eager initialization creates the instance at class load with a private static final field. It is thread-safe for free because the JVM guarantees class initialization is thread-safe, and it is my choice when the object is cheap or always needed. The synchronized getInstance method is lazy and correct, but every call pays the lock cost forever, so it becomes a bottleneck under load and I avoid it in hot paths. Double-checked locking fixes that by checking null without a lock first and only locking on the initial creation, but the instance field must be volatile, otherwise another thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor has not finished, because of instruction reordering.

For lazy loading I usually prefer the Bill Pugh holder idiom. It puts the instance inside a private static inner class that the JVM does not load until getInstance first touches it, so it is lazy, and the JVM's own class-initialization lock makes it thread-safe with no synchronization code from me. For the simplest and most bulletproof option I use the enum singleton that Joshua Bloch recommends, because the JVM guarantees a single instance and it is uniquely safe against serialization and reflection attacks that could otherwise create a second instance of the other forms. Its only limitation is that an enum cannot extend a class.

At National Bank of India we use a single shared database connection pool as a Singleton. An early version used lazy creation without proper publication, and two threads racing on startup each built a pool, which briefly doubled our connections and hit the database limit. We moved the lazy pool to the Bill Pugh holder idiom so creation is both lazy and safe, and for a cached configuration object that gets serialized we used an enum singleton so it can never be duplicated by serialization. The sentence I give interviewers is that for a thread-safe Singleton I prefer the Bill Pugh holder idiom when I want lazy initialization and the enum when I want the simplest version that is also immune to serialization and reflection, and if I ever use double-checked locking I always mark the instance field volatile.
